Latent class analysis: a complete workflow

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/workflow-lca.Rmd
workflow-lca.Rmd

Latent class analysis (LCA) is a mixture model for categorical indicators. It assumes that the observations come from a small number of unobserved classes, and that within each class the indicators are independent, each with its own response probabilities. This vignette presents a complete single-level analysis: description of the data, selection of the number of classes, estimation, interpretation, evaluation of the classification, and the relation of the classes to a distal outcome. The final section extends the model to two levels. In the output of this package the classes of observations are labelled profile_1, profile_2, and so on.

library(latents)
set.seed(1)

The estimation uses random starting values, so the seed is set once to make the results reproducible.

Data

The student_esm data contain 2,582 experience-sampling reports from university students. At each report a student indicated whether they had been engaged in each of eight activities, and rated how happy, relaxed, worried and exhausted they felt. The aim of the analysis is to identify typical combinations of activities.

activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
descriptives(student_esm, activities)
#>            variable    n n_missing mean sd min max n_distinct
#> 1 time_with_friends 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 2   on_social_media 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 3    tv_video_games 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 4    listened_music 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 5            sports 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 6           walking 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 7           reading 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2
#> 8     part_time_job 2582         0   NA NA  NA  NA          2

The reports are nested in students. The first part of this vignette treats each report as an independent observation, which corresponds to the conventional single-level model. The nesting is taken into account in the final section.

Selecting the number of classes

enumerate_lca() estimates models with one to six classes and returns the results in one table.

models <- enumerate_lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 1:6)
plot_enumeration(models)

summary(models)

The BIC is lowest for four classes, 13.2 points below the three-class model. The fourth class, however, contains 1.3% of the reports (about 32), which describe many activities at once; a class of this size is poorly supported, and the ICL, which penalizes classification uncertainty, is lower for three classes than for four. The ICL is lowest for one class, which has no uncertainty to penalize, and among the models with more than one class it is lowest for two; the two-class solution, however, has a relative entropy below 0.5 and therefore separates the reports poorly. The three-class model is retained.

Estimation

lca() fits a single-level latent class model.

fit <- lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 3)
fit
#> Latent class analysis: 3 classes
#> 2582 observations; 8 categorical indicators
#> Classes are labelled profile_1, profile_2, ... in every table.
#> Log likelihood: -7848.453248 | AIC: 15748.906 | BIC: 15901.171

Interpretation of the classes

The heatmap shows, for each class, the estimated probability that the activity was reported.

plot_profiles(fit, what = "heatmap")

The largest class, comprising 58% of the reports, is characterized by screen-based activities: social media, television and video games, and music. The smallest class, 4% of the reports, consists almost entirely of reports of working at a part-time job. The third class, 39% of the reports, has elevated probabilities of spending time with friends, walking and sport, and a probability of social media use close to zero. The same probabilities are shown below as profiles across the activities, with 95% confidence intervals where the probability is not on its boundary.

plot_responses(fit)
#> Warning: The fitted likelihood still carries a score worth 1.6% of a standard error;
#> refit with a tighter `tol` before using Wald inference.

The probabilities with their standard errors. Several are estimated at zero or one; a standard error is not defined on the boundary of the parameter space, so those are held at their bound and have none.

head(get_results(fit, "responses"), 8)
#> Warning: The fitted likelihood still carries a score worth 1.6% of a standard error;
#> refit with a tighter `tol` before using Wald inference.
#>   profile         indicator category probability threshold probability_standard_error

Classification quality

diagnostics() reports the classification measures and draws the four classification plots: the effective size of each class, the distribution of the posterior probability of each report’s assigned class, each report’s contribution to the classification entropy, and the average posterior probability matrix, which shows which classes are confused with which.

diagnostics(fit)

#> Diagnostics: Latent class analysis, 3 classes
#> 1 check needs attention: pairs dependent within a class
#> 
#> Estimation
#>   ok     best start converged                                yes                      
#>   info   best log likelihood reached by                      2 of 10 starts           
#>   ok     starts failed or unfinished                         0 of 10                  
#>   ok     estimates at a bound                                no                       
#> 
#> Class size
#>   info   smallest class                         individuals  3.6% (n = 94, class 1)   
#>   info   modal vs estimated proportions         individuals  largest gap 0.120        
#>   ok     classes with no assigned unit          individuals  0 of 3                   
#> 
#> Classification
#>   info   relative entropy                       individuals  0.662                    
#>   info   lowest average posterior               individuals  0.705 (class 3)          
#>   info   lowest odds of correct classification  individuals  3.8 (class 3)            
#> 
#> Local independence
#>   check  pairs dependent within a class                      9 of 84 tested pairs     BH-adjusted p < 0.05
#>          largest: listened_music x walking in profile_2, residual 0.110, adjusted p <1e-04; consider local_dependence = or a full covariance model
#> 
#> Information
#>   info   log likelihood, parameters, BIC                     -7848.45, 26, 15901.17   
#> 
#> Every check with its reference: get_results(x, "checks"). Other tables: get_results(x, what = ).

The relative entropy of 0.66 indicates a moderately clear classification.

Local dependence

The latent class model assumes that the activities are independent within each class. The bivariate residual of a pair of activities compares their observed co-occurrence within a class with the co-occurrence the model implies, and a large value indicates a dependence the classes do not explain. The p-value refers this Pearson statistic to a chi-square distribution that ignores the estimation of the model’s table, which makes it very conservative: in simulated data from a correctly specified latent class model it rejected 0.25% of pairs per class, and 0.08% pooled, at a nominal 5%. A pair that passes the filter below is therefore strong evidence of dependence, but a pair that does not pass it is not evidence of independence.

subset(get_results(fit, "residuals"), p_adjusted < 0.01)
#>     profile       indicator_1    indicator_2        kind observed expected residual
#> 3 profile_2    listened_music        walking categorical   0.1099 4.24e-17   0.1099
#> 4 profile_2    listened_music        reading categorical   0.0881 1.03e-16   0.0881
#> 5 profile_2            sports        walking categorical   0.0879 1.73e-16   0.0879
#> 6 profile_2    listened_music         sports categorical   0.0874 0.00e+00   0.0874
#> 8 profile_2 time_with_friends        walking categorical   0.0762 3.56e-17   0.0762
#> 9 profile_2   on_social_media listened_music categorical   0.0697 5.57e-17   0.0697
#>   effective_n statistic df  p_value p_adjusted
#> 3        1490     17.98  1 2.23e-05   2.23e-05
#> 4        1490     11.57  1 6.71e-04   6.71e-04
#> 5        1490     11.52  1 6.89e-04   6.89e-04
#> 6        1490     11.38  1 7.43e-04   7.43e-04
#> 8        1490      8.65  1 3.27e-03   3.27e-03
#> 9        1490      7.23  1 7.17e-03   7.17e-03

The largest residual is that of listening to music and walking in class 2 (18). local_dependence names pairs of categorical indicators that are modelled jointly within each class: the pair then has its own joint distribution in every class, and the other activities remain independent given the class.

dependent <- lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 3,
                 local_dependence = "listened_music:walking")
get_results(dependent, "local_dependence")
#>                      pair        kind profile         item_1 category_1  item_2
#> 1  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music         no walking
#> 2  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music         no walking
#> 3  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music        yes walking

#> 9  listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music         no walking
#> 10 listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music         no walking
#> 11 listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music        yes walking
#> 12 listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music        yes walking
#>    category_2 probability independent    ratio covariance correlation

#> 5          no    9.37e-01    0.937446 9.99e-01         NA          NA

The table gives each class’s joint probabilities of the pair beside the products of its marginal probabilities, which are the probabilities under independence, and their ratio. The two models describe the same data and are compared with compare_models().

compare_models(independent = fit, dependent = dependent)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model        Classes   k    LogLik       BIC  ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8
#> -----------  -------  --  --------  --------  ----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----
#> independent        3  26  -7848.45  15901.17  0.00   0.561  17820.27     0.66       0.71      1
#> dependent          3  29  -7836.91  15901.66  0.49   0.439  17816.33     0.66       0.70      1

The joint model raises the log likelihood by 11.5 at the cost of 3 parameters, and BIC is lower for the independent model. The dependence is present in the data, and the three classes describe the activities about as well without modelling it.

Classes and a distal outcome

three_step() estimates the mean of an outcome within each class. It uses the BCH method, which applies the inverse estimated classification-error matrix to modal class assignments (Bolck, Croon and Hagenaars, 2004). These corrected weights can be negative; posterior-probability weighting is the separate method = "proportional" option. The outcome here is the happiness rating.

happiness <- three_step(fit, student_esm, outcome = "happy")
happiness
#> Distal outcome by class (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class  Mean        95% CI     SE  Effective n
#> -----  ----  ------------  -----  -----------
#>     1  4.53  [4.22, 4.83]  0.156        88.80
#>     2  4.63  [4.53, 4.73]  0.051       957.30
#>     3  5.30  [5.16, 5.43]  0.068       549.14

Happiness is highest in the class of reports away from screens (5.30 on the seven-point scale), and lower in the screen-based class (4.63) and the work class (4.53).

Extension to two levels

Each student contributes many reports, so the reports are not independent. When the student identifier is supplied as id, multilca() estimates a two-level model: the classes of reports are retained, and the students are in addition grouped into latent classes that differ in the proportion of their reports belonging to each class.

two_level <- multilca(student_esm, activities, id = "student",
                      n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2)
get_results(two_level, "profile_probabilities")
#>   group_class profile probability group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1      0.2264                    0.36
#> 2           1       2      0.1052                    0.36
#> 3           1       3      0.6685                    0.36
#> 4           2       1      0.2513                    0.64
#> 5           2       2      0.7271                    0.64
#> 6           2       3      0.0216                    0.64

The two-level model is presented in detail in vignette("lca").

References

Bolck, A., Croon, M., & Hagenaars, J. (2004). Estimating latent structure models with categorical variables: One-step versus three-step estimators. Political Analysis, 12(1), 3–27.
